Dear Reviewers and Area Chair,

Thank you very much for the time and care you have devoted to reviewing our work. We sincerely appreciate your constructive comments and suggestions, which have helped us improve the manuscript. We have carefully considered every comment and suggestion and revised the paper accordingly, with the main changes marked in blue.

We summarize the main revisions below.

**In the main paper:**

1. Expanded the discussion of PhysicEdit, EndoCoT, and Monet to clarify their relationship with our method.
2. Clarified the roles of the latent tokens, their supervision during compression, and the separate final visual block.
3. Clarified the original backbone baseline and added image-pair fine-tuning on the same PhysTrace data.
4. Reorganized the comparisons of training data and training strategies, including their training budgets.
5. Added a method-level comparison with PhysicEdit and expanded the computation-cost comparison.
6. Clarified the sources and roles of the training and evaluation data.

**In the appendix:**

1. Added the terminal-only supervision control and its category-level results.
2. Added the comparison between time-uniform and change-uniform frame sampling.
3. Expanded the latent-representation analysis with domain probes, controlled intervention tasks, and token-order perturbations, together with their controls and limitations.
4. Expanded the discussion of general editing performance and category-level trade-offs.
5. Clarified what the model-based evaluations and human study support about physical plausibility.
6. Clarified the uncertainty of single-run results and the remaining questions about state count and the compression curriculum.

We provide detailed responses to each reviewer's comments below. Thank you again for your time and helpful suggestions.

Best regards,  
The Authors
c07ee0aff37b4477:
Thank you for highlighting PhysicEdit. We appreciate its use of video-derived transition priors to guide physical image editing without rendering intermediate videos at inference. We agree that our original discussion should have made this connection explicit, and we have expanded the related-work discussion accordingly.

**Our contribution is the progressive internalization of textual and visual process supervision into a continuous latent plan.** PhysicEdit combines an explicit textual reasoning trace at inference with video-supervised transition queries. PhysFlow progressively compresses high-level physical rationales, low-level transition descriptions, and ordered intermediate visual blocks into six latent tokens. These tokens condition the image generator together with a separate 16-token final visual block. This design internalizes the textual reasoning as well as the visual process, so inference uses the compact latent plan without decoding a textual reasoning trace. We clarify this distinction in Sections 2 and 3. [PhysicEdit, Section 3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.21778v2#S3.SS3).

**The added method-level comparison reports 56.32 for PhysFlow and 52.35 for PhysicEdit.** We evaluate PICABench-Superficial with Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and report both backbones below. We report scores on a 0 to 100 scale and gains in percentage points.

| Method | Backbone | Overall | Gain over own backbone |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 | Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 | 49.71 | N/A |
| PhysicEdit | Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 | 52.35 | +2.64 |
| Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 | Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 | 54.26 | N/A |
| **PhysFlow (Ours)** | Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 | **56.32** | **+2.06** |

PhysFlow achieves a 3.97-point higher overall score and higher scores in all eight categories. Both methods improve on their respective backbones. The different backbones make this a comparison of complete systems; isolating the contribution of each method requires a matched-backbone control. We also clarify that the existing 53.82 entry in Tables 4 and 9 refers to PhysFlow trained on PhysicTran38K; the new 52.35 entry evaluates PhysicEdit itself.

**PhysFlow also has lower latency in the reported cost comparison.**

| Method | Params (B) | Memory (GiB) | Latency (s) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| PhysicEdit | 29.00 | 56.25 | 52.19 |
| **PhysFlow (Ours)** | **28.87** | **58.11** | **49.39** |

The resource and timing measurements come from separate runs. In these reported results, PhysFlow takes 2.80 fewer seconds per edit, a 5.4% latency reduction, while using 1.86 GiB more peak memory. These measurements show a latency advantage with a memory trade-off. The revised manuscript includes the method-level results and cost comparison.

Change-uniform sampling aims to distribute supervision across visible changes in a trajectory. Appendix A.2 combines normalized DINOv2, optical-flow, and pixel-change scores, then selects four intermediate frames that divide cumulative change into approximately equal intervals. This criterion gives more temporal sampling density to portions of a clip with larger measured changes. We have added a time-uniform control using the same PhysTrace training dataset and four intermediate states, retaining progressive compression, 1,253 planner updates, and 537 generator updates. It scores 54.16% on PICABench-Superficial, compared with 56.32% for change-uniform sampling. This single-run comparison supports change-uniform sampling under the tested configuration.

We use four intermediate states as a fixed design choice, which yields four visual reasoning tokens after compression. The existing experiments evaluate this configuration. Selecting the best state count and establishing the benefit of progressive over direct compression require separate ablations. We clarify these distinctions in Appendix A.2 and report the sampling control in Appendix C.7.
fc0e159c39aa80b2:
The six latent thoughts form a learned conditioning sequence Z = [h, l, m₁, m₂, m₃, m₄] ∈ ℝ⁶ˣᵈ, where d is the planner's hidden dimension. The training design assigns h and l to high-level physical rationales and low-level transition descriptions, and assigns m₁ through m₄ to ordered intermediate visual states. The planner additionally predicts F ∈ ℝ¹⁶ˣᵈ, a final visual block. Thus, the additional conditioning consists of six reasoning tokens and 16 final-state tokens.

Section 3.4 specifies how these roles enter training. Stage I aligns each 16-token intermediate block with the corresponding frame encoding from a moving-average teacher. Stage II replaces each intermediate block with one latent token and removes that block's direct alignment loss. Later uncompressed blocks, the final visual block, and the generation objective provide the remaining supervision. After Stage II compresses all intermediate blocks, the final-block alignment and generation objectives supervise the planner. This training defines the intended roles of the latent positions, while their physical-state correspondence remains an empirical question.

**The latent plan exposes physical-domain and conditional outcome information to linear probes; token order also affects editing.** The revised Figure 7 organizes these findings into panels (a) through (d).

**(a) Token-role structure.** The original clustering visualization supports role-dependent representation structure after compression.

**(b) Physical-domain linear probe.** We fit and cross-validate a linear probe on 212 PhysTrace videos and test on 212 independent videos. The two textual and four intermediate visual tokens yield 86.91% balanced accuracy across six domains, compared with 16.67% uniform chance. The same-layout pretrained control reaches 85.94%, and the low-level text token reaches 86.79%. These controls limit attribution of domain information to PhysFlow training.

**(c) Physical-intervention prediction.** We freeze PhysFlow and fit linear ridge readouts on its four intermediate visual tokens, choosing pooling and regularization on validation data. Each synthetic source image receives two intervention instructions with opposite reference outcomes. Idealized rules define the labels; source images can display material or temperature cues. Each task uses 128 training, 32 validation, and 64 initial-test scene families. Each family supplies two source images and two instructions per image.

Pair accuracy requires both outcomes for the same image to be correct. Randomly assigning the two opposite outcomes gives 50% chance; independent binary guesses give 25%. Panel (c) displays the following seven tasks:

| Task | Pair accuracy (%) | Test pairs / families | 95% CI (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Support | 99.22 | 128 / 64 | 97.66 to 100.00 |
| Torque | 100.00 | 128 / 64 | 100.00 to 100.00 |
| Buoyancy | 99.22 | 128 / 64 | 97.66 to 100.00 |
| Outflow | 96.09 | 128 / 64 | 92.19 to 99.22 |
| Absorption | 99.22 | 128 / 64 | 97.66 to 100.00 |
| Phase change (confirmation) | 100.00 | 256 / 128 | 100.00 to 100.00 |
| Shape recovery (rubber/clay) | 91.41 | 128 / 64 | 86.72 to 96.09 |

For phase change, the table uses independent confirmation on 128 fresh families with the validation-selected probe fixed and no retuning. Intervals use 5,000 family-bootstrap draws. Perfect empirical scores produce degenerate bootstrap intervals that describe the observed families; population accuracy remains uncertain.

The seven displayed tasks form an illustrative subset of eleven exploratory tasks. The other pair accuracies are collision 50.00%, magnetic poles 28.91%, spring direction 31.25%, and foam recovery 68.75%. We retain all results and controls. This exploratory selection provides illustrative evidence with limited coverage of physical phenomena. Several tasks also reach 100% with textual latent probes or source-image probes using separate weights for each intervention condition. On phase-change confirmation, this source control reaches 91.80%, the source-and-instruction prefix reaches 92.19%, and both textual latent probes reach 100%.

**(d) Visual-token perturbation.** On 64 PICABench-Superficial inputs, eight per category, Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct gives mean accuracies of 57.36% for the original condition, 55.64% for masking, and 53.94% for both reversal and shuffling. Perturbations occur after planning, with textual and final-visual conditioning fixed. Reversal and shuffling each reduce accuracy by 3.42 percentage points, supporting order sensitivity.

Together, these results support physical-semantic and conditional-consequence readout alongside order-sensitive editing. The diagnostic scenes are synthetic. Token-to-frame temporal alignment, internal physical-law computation, and physical causal mediation through the generator require separate evidence.

We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful observation and agree that vision-language model judgments alone do not establish objective physical correctness. The GPT-based evaluations in Tables 7 and 8 address potential evaluator-family bias, and we follow the [PICABench](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17681v3#S4.SS1) and [RISEBench](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.02826v3#S2.SS2) scoring frameworks for comparable evaluation.

Our user study provides complementary human evidence: 17 participants evaluate 100 randomly sampled image-instruction pairs and favor PhysFlow over five competing methods in physical plausibility. Our case studies also examine visible physical consequences, such as updating reflections after object replacement and deforming a pillow under a dog's weight.

Together, these results support improved physical plausibility under model and human assessment. We clarify this scope and discuss physically grounded metrics as a valuable direction for future benchmarks in Appendix C.9.
25a61a9fd2174453:
**PhysFlow learns a compact plan from supervision of both the physical transformation and its outcome.** A target image specifies the desired result; physical rationales and intermediate visual states provide additional supervision about the transformation. Our contribution is a training curriculum that compresses these complementary signals into six latent tokens while retaining a separate 16-token final visual block. This allocates different representation budgets to the transformation and its endpoint, and gives the image generator access to both (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to EndoCoT, we change the representation and its supervision during compression.** EndoCoT establishes a closely related approach with recurrent thought states, intermediate image-generation supervision, and terminal textual grounding. Its terminal-consolidation stage retains recurrent thought updates while stopping gradient propagation through intermediate steps. It also avoids decoding intermediate images at inference, a property we share. [EndoCoT, Section 4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12252v1#S4.SS2). PhysFlow replaces high-level physical rationales, low-level transition descriptions, and then successive intermediate visual blocks with individual latent tokens. Each visual replacement removes that block's direct alignment loss; later uncompressed blocks, final-block alignment, and the flow-matching loss continue to train the compressed tokens. The curriculum therefore changes how the planner represents the process and receives supervision as it approaches the inference representation. At inference, the generator receives all six plan tokens together with the separate final visual block (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to Monet, we jointly internalize textual and visual process supervision for image generation.** Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning and further trains them with visual-latent policy optimization. Its latent embeddings support a model that produces textual answers. [Monet, Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3). PhysFlow compresses both the textual rationales and the intermediate visual representations into a continuous plan before generating the edited image. During planner training, the flow-matching loss propagates through a frozen image generator to train the conditioning representations. We then freeze the planner and adapt the generator to these representations. This couples learning the plan to its use in image generation (Section 3.4).

**The same-data control now measures the gain beyond adaptation to the training pairs.** PhysFlow scores 56.32 on PICABench-Superficial, compared with 55.12 for image-pair SFT on the same PhysTrace pairs. Both use the same generator LoRA configuration and 537 generator updates; PhysFlow additionally trains its planner, for 1,790 total updates. The terminal-only run scores 55.57, compared with 56.32 for full PhysFlow as reported in the paper. The 0.75-point difference compares training configurations; finer attribution to supervision and curriculum requires further controls. These comparisons report single-run point estimates. We clarify these design differences in Sections 2 and 3 and report each completed control alongside the claim it tests.
7a705a179c1e9e6d: PICA-100K provides training data, while PICABench provides a separately curated evaluation set of 900 editing examples (Pu et al., [Sections 3.1 and 3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17681v3#S3.SS2), and [Section 3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17681v3#S3.SS4)). The authors collect PICABench evaluation images from licensed and public sources and construct PICA-100K from generated source images and synthetic videos. We start constructing our PhysTrace training dataset with PICA-100K image-instruction pairs (Section 3.2 of our manuscript). We clarify these distinct data sources and their training and evaluation roles in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.

Thank you for pointing out the category-level declines. Table 6 reports an overall ImgEdit-Bench score of 4.39 for PhysFlow and 4.41 for Qwen-Image-Edit-2511. PhysFlow scores higher in six of nine categories, while the largest declines occur in Hybrid (3.76 to 3.26) and Extract (4.16 to 3.91), with a smaller decrease in Add (4.45 to 4.26).

We interpret the declines in Hybrid and Extract as task-dependent transfer from physical-process supervision. PhysTrace emphasizes causally connected state evolution within a physical process through textual rationales and intermediate visual states (Sections 3.2 to 3.4). Hybrid combines separately specified editing operations within one instruction, whereas Extract requires isolating a subject while preserving its identity and visual details. [ImgEdit, Sections 3.1 and 4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20275v1#S3.SS1).

We have revised Appendix C.1 to report these category-level declines alongside the improvements. The revised text describes similar aggregate performance with category-dependent trade-offs, replacing the original claim of general editing without compromise.

The curriculum therefore changes how the planner represents the process and receives supervision as it approaches the inference representation. At inference, the generator receives all six plan tokens together with the separate final visual block (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to Monet, we jointly internalize textual and visual process supervision for image generation.** Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning and further trains them with visual-latent policy optimization. Its latent embeddings support a model that produces textual answers. [Monet, Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3). PhysFlow compresses both the textual rationales and the intermediate visual representations into a continuous plan before generating the edited image. During planner training, the flow-matching loss propagates through a frozen image generator to train the conditioning representations. We then freeze the planner and adapt the generator to these representations. This couples learning the plan to its use in image generation (Section 3.4).

**The same-data control now measures the gain beyond adaptation to the training pairs.** PhysFlow scores 56.32 on PICABench-Superficial, compared with 55.12 for image-pair SFT on the same PhysTrace pairs. Both use the same generator LoRA configuration and 537 generator updates; PhysFlow additionally trains its planner, for 1,790 total updates. The terminal-only run scores 55.57, compared with 56.32 for full PhysFlow as reported in the paper. The 0.75-point difference compares training configurations; finer attribution to supervision and curriculum requires further controls. These comparisons report single-run point estimates. We will clarify these design differences in Sections 2 and 3 and report each control alongside the claim it tests.

Change-uniform sampling aims to distribute supervision across visible changes in a trajectory. Appendix A.2 combines normalized DINOv2, optical-flow, and pixel-change scores, then selects four intermediate frames that divide cumulative change into approximately equal intervals. This criterion gives more temporal sampling density to portions of a clip with larger measured changes. Its benefit over time-uniform sampling requires a comparison that fixes the videos, endpoints, state count, and training procedure.

We use four intermediate states as a fixed design choice, which yields four visual reasoning tokens after compression. The existing experiments evaluate this configuration. Selecting the best state count and establishing the benefit of progressive over direct compression require separate ablations. We will make these distinctions explicit when discussing the sampling rule and curriculum.

**R2.4. Latent-token roles and supervision**

Thank you for asking how the intermediate visual tokens relate to physical state transitions. We first clarify their intended roles and supervision; Point R2.5 then presents the representation analyses and controlled interventions.

The six latent thoughts form a learned conditioning sequence Z = [h, l, m₁, m₂, m₃, m₄] ∈ ℝ⁶ˣᵈ, where d is the planner's hidden dimension. The training design assigns h and l to high-level physical rationales and low-level transition descriptions, and assigns m₁ through m₄ to ordered intermediate visual states. The planner additionally predicts F ∈ ℝ¹⁶ˣᵈ, a final visual block. Thus, the additional conditioning consists of six reasoning tokens and 16 final-state tokens.

Section 3.4 specifies how these roles enter training. Stage I aligns each 16-token intermediate block with the corresponding frame encoding from a moving-average teacher. Stage II replaces each intermediate block with one latent token and removes that block's direct alignment loss. Later uncompressed blocks, the final visual block, and the generation objective provide the remaining supervision. After Stage II compresses all intermediate blocks, the final-block alignment and generation objectives supervise the planner. This training defines the intended roles of the latent positions, while their physical-state correspondence remains an empirical question.

236c6087692555e0:
**R2.8. Positioning relative to earlier latent-reasoning methods**

Thank you for highlighting the overlap with earlier latent-reasoning approaches.

**PhysFlow learns a compact plan from supervision of both the physical transformation and its outcome.** A target image specifies the desired result; physical rationales and intermediate visual states provide additional supervision about the transformation. Our contribution is a training curriculum that compresses these complementary signals into six latent tokens while retaining a separate 16-token final visual block. This allocates different representation budgets to the transformation and its endpoint, and gives the image generator access to both (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to EndoCoT, we change the representation and its supervision during compression.** EndoCoT establishes a closely related approach with recurrent thought states, intermediate image-generation supervision, and terminal textual grounding. Its terminal-consolidation stage retains recurrent thought updates while stopping gradient propagation through intermediate steps. It also avoids decoding intermediate images at inference, a property we share. [EndoCoT, Section 4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12252v1#S4.SS2). PhysFlow replaces high-level physical rationales, low-level transition descriptions, and then successive intermediate visual blocks with individual latent tokens. Each visual replacement removes that block's direct alignment loss; later uncompressed blocks, final-block alignment, and the flow-matching loss continue to train the compressed tokens. The curriculum therefore changes how the planner represents the process and receives supervision as it approaches the inference representation. At inference, the generator receives all six plan tokens together with the separate final visual block (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to Monet, we jointly internalize textual and visual process supervision for image generation.** Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning and further trains them with visual-latent policy optimization. Its latent embeddings support a model that produces textual answers. [Monet, Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3). PhysFlow compresses both the textual rationales and the intermediate visual representations into a continuous plan before generating the edited image. During planner training, the flow-matching loss propagates through a frozen image generator to train the conditioning representations. We then freeze the planner and adapt the generator to these representations. This couples learning the plan to its use in image generation (Section 3.4).

**The same-data control now measures the gain beyond adaptation to the training pairs.** PhysFlow scores 56.32 on PICABench-Superficial, compared with 55.12 for image-pair SFT on the same PhysTrace pairs. Both use the same generator LoRA configuration and 537 generator updates; PhysFlow additionally trains its planner, for 1,790 total updates. The terminal-only run scores 55.57, compared with 56.32 for full PhysFlow as reported in the paper. The 0.75-point difference compares training configurations; finer attribution to supervision and curriculum requires further controls. These comparisons report single-run point estimates. We clarify these design differences in Sections 2 and 3 and report each completed control alongside the claim it tests.

Thank you for pointing out that the dataset comparisons also involve differences in supervision and training procedure.

All four configurations use Qwen-Image-Edit-2511. We evaluate PICABench-Superficial with Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and report gains in percentage points.

| Training data | Training strategy | Overall (%) |
|---|---|---:|
| PICA100K | Image-pair SFT | 53.38 |
| PhysTrace | Image-pair SFT | 55.12 |
| PhysicTran38K | PhysFlow | 53.82 |
| PhysTrace | PhysFlow | 56.32 |

**(a) Dataset comparison under image-pair SFT: +1.74 points.** PhysTrace reaches 55.12, compared with 53.38 for PICA100K, using fewer training examples and generator updates. Both configurations use source-target image-pair supervision. This result supports the effectiveness of the PhysTrace image pairs even with direct generator fine-tuning.

**(b) Dataset comparison within PhysFlow: +2.50 points.** PhysTrace reaches 56.32, compared with 53.82 for PhysicTran38K, while using the same PhysFlow architecture and curriculum. PhysTrace again achieves a higher score with fewer training examples. The 53.82 row denotes PhysFlow trained on PhysicTran38K. Together, these two comparisons support the usefulness of the smaller PhysTrace dataset under both training strategies.

**(c) Framework comparison on the same PhysTrace pairs: +1.20 points.** PhysFlow reaches 56.32, compared with 55.12 for image-pair SFT. This comparison fixes the source-target pairs, rank-512 generator LoRA configuration, and 537 generator updates. It shows that the complete PhysFlow training framework improves on direct adaptation to the same image pairs.

**Training conditions.** Across datasets, PICA100K SFT uses 4,926 updates, PhysTrace SFT uses 537, and PhysFlow uses 4,632 on PhysicTran38K versus 1,790 on PhysTrace. PhysFlow adds planner capacity and training to the matched generator budget. These results compare the reported data and framework configurations. The terminal-only run scores 55.57, 0.75 points below the paper's reported full PhysFlow score of 56.32. We report this difference at the training-configuration level; the direct-compression control will address the curriculum separately. Thank you for identifying these missing ablations. We have added a time-uniform sampling comparison.

Change-uniform sampling selects four intermediate frames at equal intervals of cumulative visual change, using normalized DINOv2, optical-flow, and pixel-change scores (Appendix A.2).

We reran time-uniform sampling with the same PhysTrace dataset settings as change-uniform sampling. The PICABench-Superficial results are:

| Sampling | LP | LSE | RFL | RFR | DFM | CSL | GST | LST | Overall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Time-uniform | 53.72 | 63.06 | 59.30 | 58.24 | 43.29 | 46.21 | 62.35 | 53.65 | 55.09 |

c7ced1c1acc75b8e:
**Response 4. Latent-token roles and supervision**

Thank you for asking how the intermediate visual tokens relate to physical state transitions. We first clarify their intended roles and supervision; Response 5 then presents the representation analyses and controlled interventions.

The six latent thoughts form a learned conditioning sequence Z = [h, l, m₁, m₂, m₃, m₄] ∈ ℝ⁶ˣᵈ, where d is the planner's hidden dimension. The training design assigns h and l to high-level physical rationales and low-level transition descriptions, and assigns m₁ through m₄ to ordered intermediate visual states. The planner additionally predicts F ∈ ℝ¹⁶ˣᵈ, a final visual block. Thus, the additional conditioning consists of six reasoning tokens and 16 final-state tokens.

Section 3.4 specifies how these roles enter training. Stage I aligns each 16-token intermediate block with the corresponding frame encoding from a moving-average teacher. Stage II replaces each intermediate block with one latent token and removes that block's direct alignment loss. Later uncompressed blocks, the final visual block, and the generation objective provide the remaining supervision. After Stage II compresses all intermediate blocks, the final-block alignment and generation objectives supervise the planner. This training defines the intended roles of the latent positions, while their physical-state correspondence remains an empirical question.
fb08964c9893cb8a:
**Response 5. Physical information in the latent representations**

We appreciate your careful distinction between sensitivity to token order and evidence of physically meaningful representations. Following your suggestion, we have expanded Figure 7 with representation analyses and controlled intervention tasks.

**The latent plan exposes physical-domain and conditional outcome information to linear probes; token order also affects editing.** The revised Figure 7 organizes these findings into panels (a) through (d).

**(a) Token-role structure.** The original clustering visualization supports role-dependent representation structure after compression.

**(b) Physical-domain linear probe.** We fit and cross-validate a linear probe on 212 PhysTrace videos and test on 212 independent videos. The two textual and four intermediate visual tokens yield 86.91% balanced accuracy across six domains, compared with 16.67% uniform chance. The same-layout pretrained control reaches 85.94%, and the low-level text token reaches 86.79%. These controls limit attribution of domain information to PhysFlow training.

**(c) Physical-intervention prediction.** We freeze PhysFlow and fit linear ridge readouts on its four intermediate visual tokens, choosing pooling and regularization on validation data. Each synthetic source image receives two intervention instructions with opposite reference outcomes. Idealized rules define the labels; source images can display material or temperature cues. Each task uses 128 training, 32 validation, and 64 initial-test scene families. Each family supplies two source images and two instructions per image.

Pair accuracy requires both outcomes for the same image to be correct. Randomly assigning the two opposite outcomes gives 50% chance; independent binary guesses give 25%. Panel (c) displays the following seven tasks:

| Task | Pair accuracy (%) | Test pairs / families | 95% CI (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Support | 99.22 | 128 / 64 | 97.66 to 100.00 |
| Torque | 100.00 | 128 / 64 | 100.00 to 100.00 |
| Buoyancy | 99.22 | 128 / 64 | 97.66 to 100.00 |
| Outflow | 96.09 | 128 / 64 | 92.19 to 99.22 |
| Absorption | 99.22 | 128 / 64 | 97.66 to 100.00 |
| Phase change (confirmation) | 100.00 | 256 / 128 | 100.00 to 100.00 |
| Shape recovery (rubber/clay) | 91.41 | 128 / 64 | 86.72 to 96.09 |

For phase change, the table uses independent confirmation on 128 fresh families with the validation-selected probe fixed and no retuning. Intervals use 5,000 family-bootstrap draws. Perfect empirical scores produce degenerate bootstrap intervals that describe the observed families; population accuracy remains uncertain.

The seven displayed tasks form an illustrative subset of eleven exploratory tasks. The other pair accuracies are collision 50.00%, magnetic poles 28.91%, spring direction 31.25%, and foam recovery 68.75%. We retain all results and controls. This exploratory selection provides illustrative evidence with limited coverage of physical phenomena. Several tasks also reach 100% with textual latent probes or source-image probes using separate weights for each intervention condition. On phase-change confirmation, this source control reaches 91.80%, the source-and-instruction prefix reaches 92.19%, and both textual latent probes reach 100%.

**(d) Visual-token perturbation.** On 64 PICABench-Superficial inputs, eight per category, Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct gives mean accuracies of 57.36% for the original condition, 55.64% for masking, and 53.94% for both reversal and shuffling. Perturbations occur after planning, with textual and final-visual conditioning fixed. Reversal and shuffling each reduce accuracy by 3.42 percentage points, supporting order sensitivity.

Together, these results support physical-semantic and conditional-consequence readout alongside order-sensitive editing. The diagnostic scenes are synthetic. Token-to-frame temporal alignment, internal physical-law computation, and physical causal mediation through the generator require separate evidence.

afab3397ddc66b8d:
**Response 7. Multimodal-model evaluation and human evidence**

Thank you for raising this concern about multimodal-model judgments. Your comment prompted us to clarify the roles of the model-based evaluations, the human study, and the qualitative examples.

We agree that vision-language model judgments alone do not establish objective physical correctness. The GPT-based evaluations in Tables 7 and 8 address potential evaluator-family bias, and we follow the [PICABench](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17681v3#S4.SS1) and [RISEBench](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.02826v3#S2.SS2) scoring frameworks for comparable evaluation.

Our user study provides complementary human evidence: 17 participants evaluate 100 randomly sampled image-instruction pairs and favor PhysFlow over five competing methods in physical plausibility. Our case studies also examine visible physical consequences, such as updating reflections after object replacement and deforming a pillow under a dog's weight.

We clarify the evaluation scope and discuss physically grounded metrics as a valuable direction for future benchmarks in Appendix C.9. Together, the model-based evaluations and our human study support improved physical plausibility.
7df9c0db8cfadfa5:
**Response 8. Positioning relative to earlier latent-reasoning methods**

Thank you for highlighting the overlap with earlier latent-reasoning approaches.

**PhysFlow learns a compact plan from supervision of both the physical transformation and its outcome.** A target image specifies the desired result; physical rationales and intermediate visual states provide additional supervision about the transformation. Our contribution is a training curriculum that compresses these complementary signals into six latent tokens while retaining a separate 16-token final visual block. This allocates different representation budgets to the transformation and its endpoint, and gives the image generator access to both (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to EndoCoT, we change the representation and its supervision during compression.** EndoCoT establishes a closely related approach with recurrent thought states, intermediate image-generation supervision, and terminal textual grounding. Its terminal-consolidation stage retains recurrent thought updates while stopping gradient propagation through intermediate steps. It also avoids decoding intermediate images at inference, a property we share. [EndoCoT, Section 4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12252v1#S4.SS2). PhysFlow replaces high-level physical rationales, low-level transition descriptions, and then successive intermediate visual blocks with individual latent tokens. Each visual replacement removes that block's direct alignment loss; later uncompressed blocks, final-block alignment, and the flow-matching loss continue to train the compressed tokens. The curriculum therefore changes how the planner represents the process and receives supervision as it approaches the inference representation. At inference, the generator receives all six plan tokens together with the separate final visual block (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to Monet, we jointly internalize textual and visual process supervision for image generation.** Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning and further trains them with visual-latent policy optimization. Its latent embeddings support a model that produces textual answers. [Monet, Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3). PhysFlow compresses both the textual rationales and the intermediate visual representations into a continuous plan before generating the edited image. During planner training, the flow-matching loss propagates through a frozen image generator to train the conditioning representations. We then freeze the planner and adapt the generator to these representations. This couples learning the plan to its use in image generation (Section 3.4).

**The same-data control now measures the gain beyond adaptation to the training pairs.** PhysFlow scores 56.32 on PICABench-Superficial, compared with 55.12 for image-pair SFT on the same PhysTrace pairs. Both use the same generator LoRA configuration and 537 generator updates; PhysFlow additionally trains its planner, for 1,790 total updates. The terminal-only run scores 55.57, compared with 56.32 for full PhysFlow as reported in the paper. The 0.75-point difference compares training configurations; finer attribution to supervision and curriculum requires further controls. These comparisons report single-run point estimates. We clarify these design differences in Sections 2 and 3 and report each completed control alongside the claim it tests.

1aedf16543f0acdc:
Thank you very much for pointing out the missing discussion of PhysicEdit. We apologize for this omission and have added the discussion to Section 2.2, “Visual Transition Modeling for Image Editing,” in Related Work.

We appreciate [PhysicEdit's thoughtful design](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.21778v2#S3.SS3) and share its view that textual explanations and visual trajectories provide complementary forms of intermediate reasoning. Text describes the physical principles and causal relationships behind an edit, while visual trajectories describe how the scene changes. This common perspective underlies both approaches. At inference, PhysicEdit combines an explicit textual reasoning trace with latent visual representations produced by learned transition queries.

**Our specific focus, however, is to progressively internalize the text-to-visual reasoning process into an ordered latent plan:**

1. **Text-derived physical constraints guide visual prediction.** The planner first predicts latent states for physical principles and transition steps. It then predicts visual latents conditioned on these states and preceding visual latents, allowing physical reasoning to guide visual prediction within the planner.

2. **Visual supervision shapes the reasoning states.** During planner training, downstream visual prediction and editing losses propagate through the continuous latent sequence to train earlier states. This encourages the text-derived states to retain information useful for the intended visual changes.

3. **Progressive compression internalizes both forms of reasoning.** We gradually replace explicit textual reasoning and intermediate visual blocks with latent tokens while retaining downstream visual and editing supervision. At inference, the resulting compact plan guides editing without decoding an explicit textual reasoning trace.

The resulting plan contains six latent tokens, Z = [h, l, m₁, m₂, m₃, m₄]. The training design assigns h to high-level physical rationales, l to low-level transition descriptions, and m₁ through m₄ to the ordered intermediate visual stages used during training. A separate 16-token final visual block provides final-state conditioning. We have clarified this design and these token roles in Section 3.

To better explain what these tokens retain after compression, we have expanded the four-part analysis in Figure 7:

- **(a) Token-role structure.** Different reasoning roles occupy distinct regions in a shared principal-component projection, supporting role-dependent representation structure after compression.
- **(b) Physical-domain information.** A linear probe on the six latent tokens reaches 86.91% balanced accuracy across six physical domains on 212 held-out videos (same-layout pretrained control: 85.94%), showing that physical-domain information remains accessible after compression.
- **(c) Physical-intervention prediction.** Across 11 exploratory synthetic tasks, probes on the four visual tokens predict both outcomes in same-image intervention pairs. Seven selected tasks reach 91.41–100% pair accuracy; the other four reach 28.91–68.75%. A fixed phase-change probe also reaches 100% on 256 pairs from 128 new confirmation families.
- **(d) Token-order sensitivity.** On 64 PICABench-Superficial inputs, reversing or shuffling the intermediate visual tokens reduces mean accuracy from 57.36% to 53.94%, with textual and final-visual conditioning fixed. This 3.42-point decrease supports sensitivity to the ordering of the intermediate tokens.

The appendix includes the full task set and input/text controls. Together, these analyses provide evidence of role-dependent structure, readable physical-domain and conditional-outcome information, and order-sensitive editing in our compressed representation.

**Following your helpful suggestion, we have also added an experimental comparison with PhysicEdit on PICABench-Superficial.** We use Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct for evaluation. Our PhysFlow implementation uses Qwen-Image-Edit-2511.

| Method | LP | LSE | RFL | RFR | DFM | CSL | GST | LST | Overall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| PhysicEdit | 51.62 | 61.63 | 51.56 | 52.96 | 44.03 | 45.89 | 57.64 | 53.07 | 52.35 |
| **PhysFlow (Ours)** | **54.45** | **65.19** | **58.52** | **57.99** | **44.91** | **47.31** | **64.32** | **56.43** | **56.32** |

In this evaluation, PhysFlow achieves an overall score of **56.32**, compared with **52.35** for PhysicEdit, with higher scores across all eight categories. We have incorporated these results into Table 1 and added a computational-cost comparison in Table 5.

We sincerely appreciate your suggestion, which helped us present the relationship to PhysicEdit and the evidence for our latent representation more clearly.

**Response 7. Multimodal-model evaluation and human evidence**

Thank you very much for raising this concern about objective physical correctness. We appreciate your emphasis on the physical basis of our evaluation.

**(1) PICABench specifies physical criteria for each editing example.** Its PICAEval protocol uses human-annotated regions and manually reviewed yes/no questions about physical consequences, such as whether object removal also removes its shadow. A vision-language model (VLM) answers these questions by inspecting the edited image, and accuracy measures exact agreement with predefined reference answers. Thus, the benchmark's task design and annotations specify the physical requirements, while the VLM checks their visible consequences ([PICABench, Section 3.3 and Appendix A.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17681v3#S3.SS3)).

**(2) Our human study provides complementary evidence.** We ask 17 participants to compare PhysFlow with five competing methods on 100 image-instruction pairs randomly sampled from PICABench and RISEBench. Participants favor PhysFlow in physical plausibility. This overall trend is consistent with our benchmark findings and provides human support for improved physical plausibility.
87f92925ae58ba29:
**Response 8. Originality and positioning relative to closely related approaches**

Thank you very much for carefully examining the originality of our work. We acknowledge the inspiration from prior work on progressive chain-of-thought internalization, continuous latent reasoning, and visual feature prediction. **PhysFlow contributes a joint internalization framework that turns textual physical reasoning and visual state transitions into a continuous latent plan for image editing.** We clarify its motivation and methodological distinctions below.

**(1) A joint representation connects physical constraints with visual changes.** Physics-aware editing requires a model to connect the physical relations governing an edit with their consequences in image space. Textual rationales express these relations, while intermediate visual states specify how the scene changes. PhysFlow learns from both and progressively internalizes them into a compact plan. This design allows textual physical reasoning to guide visual state prediction within the planner, before the generator renders the edited image (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**(2) Our internalization procedure differs from the closely related approaches.** [Monet](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3) retains text-latent interleaved reasoning for textual answers. [EndoCoT](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12252v1#S4.SS2) iteratively refines latent states and uses textual reasoning to align the terminal state. PhysFlow progressively replaces both explicit textual rationales and ordered intermediate visual blocks with latent tokens. As each intermediate visual block becomes a latent token, we remove its direct alignment loss and continue training through downstream visual and image-generation objectives. This curriculum teaches the planner to use compressed textual and visual information together. [PhysicEdit](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.21778v1#S3.SS3) retains explicit textual reasoning and updates its transition queries exclusively through its visual transition loss. In PhysFlow, the final-image generation loss also propagates through the frozen generator into the planner during internalization, directly training the latent plan for its use in editing (Section 3.4).

**(3) PhysTrace supplies the process supervision for this framework.** We construct 11,448 synthetic trajectories that pair hierarchical physical rationales with ordered intermediate visual states and editing targets. These annotations provide the textual and visual process supervision that the joint internalization curriculum requires (Section 3.2).

**To our knowledge, PhysFlow is the first framework to jointly internalize textual physical reasoning and intermediate visual state transitions into a unified continuous latent plan for physics-aware image editing.** This contribution concerns the joint representation and its learning procedure.

2e8afe37530ad2b3:
**Response 4: Latent-token roles and supervision**

Thank you for asking how the intermediate visual tokens relate to physical state transitions. We first clarify their intended roles and supervision; Response 5 then presents the representation analyses and controlled interventions.

The six-token sequence Z = [h, l, m₁, m₂, m₃, m₄] assigns h and l to high-level physical rationales and low-level transition descriptions, and m₁ through m₄ to ordered intermediate visual states. A separate final visual block F contains 16 tokens.

In Stage I, each 16-token intermediate block aligns with its frame encoding from a moving-average teacher. Stage II replaces these blocks sequentially with single latent tokens and removes each replaced block's direct alignment loss. **Response 7: Multimodal-model evaluation and human evidence**

Thank you very much for raising this concern about objective physical correctness. We appreciate your emphasis on the physical basis of our evaluation.

**(1) PICABench specifies physical criteria for each editing example.** Its PICAEval protocol uses human-annotated regions and manually reviewed yes/no questions about physical consequences, such as whether object removal also removes its shadow. A vision-language model (VLM) answers these questions by inspecting the edited image, and accuracy measures exact agreement with predefined reference answers. Thus, the benchmark's task design and annotations specify the physical requirements, while the VLM checks their visible consequences ([PICABench, Section 3.3 and Appendix A.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17681v3#S3.SS3)).

**(2) Our human study provides complementary evidence.** We ask 17 participants to compare PhysFlow with five competing methods on 100 image-instruction pairs randomly sampled from PICABench and RISEBench. Participants favor PhysFlow in physical plausibility. This overall trend is consistent with our benchmark findings and provides human support for improved physical plausibility.
c53fb9885625fc4f:
**Response 8: Originality and positioning relative to closely related approaches**

Thank you very much for carefully examining the originality of our work. We acknowledge the inspiration from prior work on progressive chain-of-thought internalization, continuous latent reasoning, and visual feature prediction. **PhysFlow contributes a joint internalization framework that turns textual physical reasoning and visual state transitions into a continuous latent plan for image editing.** We clarify its motivation and methodological distinctions below.

**(1) Textual physical reasoning guides visual evolution.** Textual rationales describe physical relations and causal dependencies; intermediate visual states describe their consequences. PhysFlow progressively internalizes both into a continuous latent sequence in which textual latents guide subsequent visual latents before image generation (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**(2) Our internalization procedure differs from the closely related approaches.** [Monet](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3) retains text-latent interleaved reasoning for textual answers. [EndoCoT](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12252v1#S4.SS2) iteratively refines latent states and uses textual reasoning to align the terminal state. PhysFlow progressively replaces both explicit textual rationales and ordered intermediate visual blocks with latent tokens. As each intermediate visual block becomes a latent token, we remove its direct alignment loss and continue training through downstream visual and image-generation objectives. This curriculum teaches the planner to use compressed textual and visual information together. [PhysicEdit](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.21778v1#S3.SS3) retains explicit textual reasoning and updates its transition queries exclusively through its visual transition loss. In PhysFlow, the final-image generation loss also propagates through the frozen generator into the planner during internalization, directly training the latent plan for its use in editing (Section 3.4).

**(3) PhysTrace supplies process supervision.** Its 11,448 synthetic trajectories pair hierarchical physical rationales, ordered intermediate visual states, and editing targets for this curriculum (Section 3.2).

**To our knowledge, PhysFlow is the first framework to jointly internalize textual physical reasoning and intermediate visual state transitions into a unified continuous latent plan for physics-aware image editing.**

Thank you for asking us to clarify the contribution. **PhysFlow internalizes the connection between physical explanations and visual evolution into a latent plan for image editing.** Textual rationales explain the physical rules and transition steps; intermediate visual states supervise how those steps change the scene. Our curriculum progressively compresses both into a continuous plan that conditions image generation (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

**Relative to EndoCoT, our distinction lies in how explicit process supervision becomes a latent plan.** EndoCoT trains recurrent thought states with intermediate image-generation losses and terminal textual grounding, then shifts optimization to the terminal step. [EndoCoT, Section 4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12252v1#S4.SS2). PhysFlow first learns explicit textual rationales and visual trajectories, then progressively replaces their textual and visual blocks with latent tokens. Text-derived states precede and condition subsequent visual states, while downstream visual and editing losses train the compressed sequence. This curriculum teaches the planner to carry physical explanations forward into visual evolution as explicit reasoning disappears.

**Relative to Monet, we train the latent plan through the image transformation it guides.** Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning for textual answers. [Monet, Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3). PhysFlow jointly compresses textual rationales and visual trajectories, and propagates the image-generation loss through the generator to train the plan. The plan therefore receives supervision from both the physical process and the edited outcome. Responses 3 and 4 report the same-data SFT and terminal-only controls.

8f8c6e9c04a0a9b7:
Dear Reviewer xuAm,

Thank you for your careful reading and constructive feedback. Your requests for additional experiments, direct method comparisons, and methodological clarifications have helped us strengthen the experimental evidence and improve the clarity and quality of the manuscript. We address your comments point by point below.

**Response 1: Central contribution relative to EndoCoT and Monet**

Thank you for asking us to clarify the contribution. PhysFlow internalizes the connection between physical explanations and visual evolution into a latent plan for image editing. Textual rationales explain the physical rules and transition steps; intermediate visual states supervise how those steps change the scene. Our curriculum progressively compresses both into a continuous plan that conditions image generation (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

Relative to EndoCoT, our distinction lies in how explicit process supervision becomes a latent plan. EndoCoT trains recurrent thought states with intermediate image-generation losses and terminal textual grounding, then shifts optimization to the terminal step. [EndoCoT, Section 4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12252v1#S4.SS2). PhysFlow first learns explicit textual rationales and visual trajectories, then progressively replaces their textual and visual blocks with latent tokens. Text-derived states precede and condition subsequent visual states, while downstream visual and editing losses train the compressed sequence. This curriculum teaches the planner to carry physical explanations forward into visual evolution as explicit reasoning disappears.

Relative to Monet, we train the latent plan through the image transformation it guides. Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning for textual answers. [Monet, Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21395v2#S3). PhysFlow jointly compresses textual rationales and visual trajectories, and propagates the image-generation loss through the generator to train the plan. The plan therefore receives supervision from both the physical process and the edited outcome. Responses 3 and 4 report the same-data SFT and terminal-only controls.

e0090b92e3853222:
**Response 5: Physical information in the latent representations**

We appreciate your careful distinction between sensitivity to token order and evidence of physically meaningful representations. Following your suggestion, we have conducted three additional experiments to analyze the latent representations and visualized their results in Figure 7.

(a) Token-role structure. The original clustering visualization supports role-dependent representation structure after compression.

(b) Physical-domain linear probe. To test whether the latents retain physical-domain information, we use PhysTrace's original taxonomy, which groups 26 subcategories into six domains: optics and lighting, rigid-body motion, deformation and fracture, fluid dynamics, state change, and environment and aerodynamics. We fit and cross-validate a linear probe on 212 PhysTrace videos and test on 212 independent videos. The six latent tokens yield 86.91% balanced accuracy (mean recall across the six domains); uniform random guessing gives 1/6 = 16.67%. The same-layout pretrained control scores 85.94%, and the low-level text token scores 86.79%. These controls limit attribution to PhysFlow training.

(c) Physical-intervention prediction. We freeze PhysFlow and fit linear ridge readouts on its four intermediate visual tokens, choosing pooling and regularization on validation data. Each synthetic source image receives two intervention instructions with opposite reference outcomes. Idealized rules define the labels; source images can display material or temperature cues. Each task uses 128 training, 32 validation, and 64 initial-test scene families. Each family supplies two source images and two instructions per image.

Pair accuracy requires both outcomes for the same image to be correct. Randomly assigning the two opposite outcomes gives 50% chance; independent binary guesses give 25%. Panel (c) displays the following seven tasks:

|Task|Pair accuracy (%)|Test pairs / families|95% CI (%)|
|---|---:|---:|---|
|Support|99.22|128 / 64|97.66 to 100.00|
|Torque|100.00|128 / 64|100.00 to 100.00|
|Buoyancy|99.22|128 / 64|97.66 to 100.00|
|Outflow|96.09|128 / 64|92.19 to 99.22|
|Absorption|99.22|128 / 64|97.66 to 100.00|
|Phase change (confirmation)|100.00|256 / 128|100.00 to 100.00|
|Shape recovery (rubber/clay)|91.41|128 / 64|86.72 to 96.09|

Phase change uses 128 fresh confirmation families with the validation-selected probe fixed. Intervals use 5,000 family-bootstrap draws; perfect empirical scores yield degenerate intervals, leaving population accuracy uncertain.

The seven displayed tasks form an illustrative subset of eleven exploratory tasks. The other pair accuracies are collision 50.00%, magnetic poles 28.91%, spring direction 31.25%, and foam recovery 68.75%. We retain all results and controls. This exploratory selection provides illustrative evidence with limited coverage of physical phenomena. Several tasks also reach 100% with textual latent probes or source-image probes using separate weights for each intervention condition. On phase-change confirmation, this source control reaches 91.80%, the source-and-instruction prefix reaches 92.19%, and both textual latent probes reach 100%.

(d) Visual-token perturbation. On 64 PICABench-Superficial inputs, eight per category, Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct gives mean accuracies of 57.36% for the original condition, 55.64% for masking, and 53.94% for both reversal and shuffling. Perturbations occur after planning, with textual and final-visual conditioning fixed. Reversal and shuffling each reduce accuracy by 3.42 percentage points, supporting order sensitivity.

These results support physical-semantic and conditional-consequence readout and order-sensitive editing. The diagnostic scenes are synthetic; token-to-frame alignment, internal physical-law computation, and causal mediation through the generator remain unestablished.

(a) Token-role structure. The original clustering visualization supports role-dependent representation structure after compression.

(b) Physical-domain linear probe. To test whether the latents retain physical-domain information, we use PhysTrace's original taxonomy, which groups 26 subcategories into six domains: optics and lighting, rigid-body motion, deformation and fracture, fluid dynamics, state change, and environment and aerodynamics. We fit and cross-validate a linear probe on 212 PhysTrace videos and test on 212 independent videos. The six latent tokens yield 86.91% balanced accuracy (mean recall across the six domains); uniform random guessing gives 1/6 = 16.67%. The same-layout pretrained control scores 85.94%, and the low-level text token scores 86.79%. These controls limit attribution to PhysFlow training.

(c) Physical-intervention prediction. We test whether the visual latents distinguish different physical consequences when the instruction changes but the source image stays the same. For example, removing the block supporting a ball should make it fall, whereas removing the other block should leave it at rest. These are synthetic scenes with reference outcomes defined by idealized physical rules; some include material or temperature cues.

With PhysFlow frozen, we train a linear probe on its four intermediate visual tokens to predict each intervention's outcome, selecting the probe settings on validation data. A pair counts as correct only when the probe predicts both outcomes correctly. Figure 7(c) reports the following seven tasks:

|Task|Support|Torque|Buoyancy|Outflow|Absorption|Phase change|Shape recovery|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Pair accuracy (%)|99.22|100.00|99.22|96.09|99.22|100.00|91.41|

Phase change uses 128 fresh confirmation scene families with the validation-selected probe fixed. Shape recovery tests rubber versus clay.

The seven displayed tasks form an illustrative subset of eleven exploratory tasks. The other pair accuracies are collision 50.00%, magnetic poles 28.91%, spring direction 31.25%, and foam recovery 68.75%. We retain all results and controls. This exploratory selection provides illustrative evidence with limited coverage of physical phenomena. Several tasks also reach 100% with textual latent probes or source-image probes using separate weights for each intervention condition. On phase-change confirmation, this source control reaches 91.80%, the source-and-instruction prefix reaches 92.19%, and both textual latent probes reach 100%.

(d) Visual-token perturbation. On 64 PICABench-Superficial inputs, eight per category, Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct gives mean accuracies of 57.36% for the original condition, 55.64% for masking, and 53.94% for both reversal and shuffling. Perturbations occur after planning, with textual and final-visual conditioning fixed. Reversal and shuffling each reduce accuracy by 3.42 percentage points, supporting order sensitivity.

These results support physical-semantic and conditional-consequence readout and order-sensitive editing. The diagnostic scenes are synthetic; token-to-frame alignment, internal physical-law computation, and causal mediation through the generator remain unestablished.

15d38047d5d3383a:
**Response 7: Multimodal-model evaluation and human evidence**

Thank you very much for raising this concern about objective physical correctness. We appreciate your emphasis on the physical basis of our evaluation, which is essential for reliably assessing physics-aware image editing.

(1) PICABench specifies physical criteria for each editing example. Its PICAEval protocol uses human-annotated regions and manually reviewed yes/no questions about physical consequences, such as whether object removal also removes its shadow. A vision-language model (VLM) answers these questions by inspecting the edited image, and accuracy measures exact agreement with predefined reference answers. Thus, the benchmark's task design and annotations specify the physical requirements, while the VLM checks their visible consequences ([PICABench, Section 3.3 and Appendix A.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17681v3#S3.SS3)).

(2) Our human study provides complementary evidence. We ask 17 participants to compare PhysFlow with five competing methods on 100 image-instruction pairs randomly sampled from PICABench and RISEBench. Participants favor PhysFlow in physical plausibility. This overall trend is consistent with our benchmark findings and provides human support for improved physical plausibility.

f22807c5f20d95dd:
**Response 8: Originality and positioning relative to closely related approaches**

Thank you very much for carefully examining the originality of our work. We acknowledge the inspiration from prior work on progressive chain-of-thought internalization, continuous latent reasoning, and visual feature prediction.

(1) We learn the connection between physical explanations and visual evolution within the latent sequence. PhysicEdit retains explicit textual reasoning and trains transition queries with a frozen reasoning MLLM. In PhysFlow, textual latents guide subsequent visual latents through causal dependencies. During planner training, downstream visual losses and the image-generation loss through the frozen generator train the earlier reasoning states (Sections 3.3 and 3.4). Physical reasoning therefore guides visual evolution and is itself shaped by the transformation it must produce.

(2) Our curriculum changes both the representation and its supervision during compression. EndoCoT supervises recurrent thought states with intermediate image-generation losses and terminal textual grounding, then shifts optimization to the terminal step; Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning for textual answers. PhysFlow progressively replaces textual rationales and then ordered visual blocks with latent tokens. Each visual replacement removes that block's direct alignment loss, while downstream visual and editing supervision continues to train the compressed sequence (Section 3.4). The resulting compact plan carries both forms of process reasoning into image generation without decoding textual rationales or intermediate images.

(3) PhysTrace supplies the process supervision required for joint internalization. Its 11,448 synthetic trajectories pair hierarchical physical rationales, ordered intermediate visual states, and editing targets (Section 3.2). These aligned signals extend supervision beyond source-target pairs: they explain the physical principles, trace how the scene changes, and specify the intended outcome. PhysTrace thus trains the planner on how a physical edit unfolds, as well as what it should produce.

Together, PhysFlow turns complementary textual and visual process supervision into a unified, compact latent plan trained directly for image editing.

Thank you very much for pointing out the missing discussion of PhysicEdit. We apologize for this omission and have added the discussion to Section 2.2, “Visual Transition Modeling for Image Editing,” in Related Work.

At inference, [PhysicEdit](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.21778v2#S3.SS3) combines an explicit textual reasoning trace with latent visual representations produced by learned transition queries. We find this design particularly compelling because it connects explicit physical constraints with video-derived transition priors without requiring intermediate-video generation. We share the motivation behind this design: textual explanations and visual trajectories provide complementary forms of intermediate reasoning, with text explaining physical principles and causal relationships, and visual trajectories describing how the scene changes.

Our specific focus, however, is to progressively internalize the text-to-visual reasoning process into an ordered latent plan:

1. Textual physical reasoning guides visual evolution through causal dependencies within the latent sequence. The planner first predicts textual latent states for high-level physical rules and causal dependencies, followed by low-level transition steps. These continuous textual states guide the generation of subsequent visual latents through causal dependencies within the latent sequence. Each visual latent also builds on preceding visual latents, linking physical reasoning to successive stages of visual evolution.

2. Visual supervision shapes the reasoning states. During planner training, downstream visual prediction and editing losses propagate through the continuous latent sequence to train earlier states. This encourages the text-derived states to retain information useful for the intended visual changes.

3. Our training curriculum progressively internalizes textual and visual reasoning. PhysicEdit trains transition queries against video-derived visual features while keeping its reasoning MLLM frozen. PhysFlow first trains the planner with explicit textual rationales and intermediate visual states. We then progressively replace high-level physical rationales, low-level transition descriptions, and successive intermediate visual blocks with latent tokens. Finally, we freeze the planner and adapt the image generator to the learned continuous latent sequence. By jointly internalizing textual physical reasoning and visual evolution, this curriculum equips PhysFlow with a unified latent reasoning process that guides image editing without decoding textual rationales or intermediate images at inference.

To provide empirical support for our latent reasoning design, we have expanded the representation analyses in Figure 7. Visualizations reveal role-dependent structure, while probing studies recover physical-domain information and reveal outcome-predictive information on several controlled intervention tasks. Token-order perturbations also show that editing performance is sensitive to the ordering of intermediate visual latents. Together, these analyses help explain the physical content and functional role of our compressed plan; the appendix provides detailed results and controls.

Following your helpful suggestion, we have also added an experimental comparison with PhysicEdit on PICABench-Superficial. We use Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct for evaluation. The reported PhysFlow results use Qwen-Image-Edit-2511; results with Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 are pending.

40dda68647c8e462:
**Response 5: Physical information in the latent representations**

We appreciate your careful distinction between sensitivity to token order and evidence of physically meaningful representations. Following your suggestion, we have conducted three additional experiments to analyze the latent representations and visualized their results in Figure 7.

(a) Token-role structure. The original clustering visualization supports role-dependent representation structure after compression.

(b) Physical-domain linear probe. To test whether the latents retain physical-domain information, we use PhysTrace's original taxonomy, which groups 26 subcategories into six domains: optics and lighting, rigid-body motion, deformation and fracture, fluid dynamics, state change, and environment and aerodynamics. We fit and cross-validate a linear probe on 212 PhysTrace videos and test on 212 independent videos. The six latent tokens yield 86.91% balanced accuracy (mean recall across the six domains); uniform random guessing gives 1/6 = 16.67%. The same-layout pretrained control scores 85.94%, and the low-level text token scores 86.79%. These controls limit attribution to PhysFlow training.

(c) Physical-intervention prediction. We test whether the visual latents distinguish different physical consequences when the instruction changes but the source image stays the same. For example, removing the block supporting a ball should make it fall, whereas removing the other block should leave it at rest. These are synthetic scenes with reference outcomes defined by idealized physical rules; some include material or temperature cues.

With PhysFlow frozen, we train a linear probe on its four intermediate visual tokens to predict each intervention's outcome, selecting the probe settings on validation data. A pair counts as correct only when the probe predicts both outcomes correctly. Figure 7(c) reports the following seven tasks:

|Task|Support|Torque|Buoyancy|Outflow|Absorption|Phase change|Shape recovery|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Pair accuracy (%)|99.22|100.00|99.22|96.09|99.22|100.00|91.41|

Phase change uses 128 fresh confirmation scene families with the validation-selected probe fixed. Shape recovery tests rubber versus clay.

Linear probes on our intermediate visual latents achieve 91.41%–100% pair accuracy on the seven illustrated tasks, selected from eleven exploratory tasks. These results demonstrate that the visual latents encode information useful for predicting the physical consequences of interventions (Appendix C.6).

(d) Visual-token perturbation. On 64 PICABench-Superficial inputs, eight per category, Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct gives mean accuracies of 57.36% for the original condition, 55.64% for masking, and 53.94% for both reversal and shuffling. Perturbations occur after planning, with textual and final-visual conditioning fixed. Reversal and shuffling each reduce accuracy by 3.42 percentage points, supporting order sensitivity.

The four analyses show that (a) the latent space is organized by token role; (b) physical-domain information is linearly decodable; (c) linear probes accurately predict intervention outcomes from the visual latents on the illustrated tasks; and (d) visual-token order affects editing performance.

Together, these results demonstrate that PhysFlow's compact latent plan encodes the structured, physically relevant information that our design aims to preserve.

5f2988c526bf7323:
Dear Reviewer xuAm,

We sincerely thank you for the time and effort you devoted to reviewing our manuscript and for your detailed, constructive feedback. We especially appreciate your suggestions for additional experiments, direct method comparisons, and clearer explanations of our approach. Your comments have helped us recognize where the original manuscript needed fuller explanations and stronger evidence, and have guided us in improving its clarity and quality. We have carefully considered each of your concerns and respond point by point below.

**Response 1: Central contribution relative to EndoCoT and Monet**

Thank you for asking us to clarify the contribution. PhysFlow internalizes the connection between physical explanations and visual evolution into a latent plan for image editing. Textual rationales explain the physical rules and transition steps; intermediate visual states supervise how those steps change the scene. Our curriculum progressively compresses both into a continuous plan that conditions image generation (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

Relative to EndoCoT, our distinction lies in how explicit process supervision becomes a latent plan. EndoCoT trains recurrent thought states with intermediate image-generation losses and terminal textual grounding, then shifts optimization to the terminal step. EndoCoT, Section 4.2. PhysFlow first learns explicit textual rationales and visual trajectories, then progressively replaces their textual and visual blocks with latent tokens. Text-derived states precede and condition subsequent visual states, while downstream visual and editing losses train the compressed sequence. This curriculum teaches the planner to carry physical explanations forward into visual evolution as explicit reasoning disappears.

Relative to Monet, we train the latent plan through the image transformation it guides. Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning for textual answers. Monet, Section 3. PhysFlow jointly compresses textual rationales and visual trajectories, and propagates the image-generation loss through the generator to train the plan. The plan therefore receives supervision from both the physical process and the edited outcome. Responses 3 and 4 report the same-data SFT and terminal-only controls.

5ff30133eaff5b9f:
**Response 6: Multimodal-model evaluation and human evidence**

Thank you very much for raising this concern about objective physical correctness. We appreciate your emphasis on the physical basis of our evaluation, which is essential for reliably assessing physics-aware image editing.

(1) PICABench specifies physical criteria for each editing example. Its PICAEval protocol uses human-annotated regions and manually reviewed yes/no questions about physical consequences, such as whether object removal also removes its shadow. A vision-language model (VLM) answers these questions by inspecting the edited image, and accuracy measures exact agreement with predefined reference answers. Thus, the benchmark's task design and annotations specify the physical requirements, while the VLM checks their visible consequences (PICABench, Section 3.3 and Appendix A.3).

(2) Our human study also provides complementary evidence. We ask 17 participants to compare PhysFlow with five competing methods on 100 image-instruction pairs randomly sampled from PICABench and RISEBench. Participants favor PhysFlow in physical plausibility. This overall trend is consistent with our benchmark findings and provides human support for improved physical plausibility.

**Response 7: Originality and positioning relative to closely related approaches**

Thank you very much for carefully examining the originality of our work. We acknowledge the inspiration from prior work on progressive chain-of-thought internalization, continuous latent reasoning, and visual feature prediction.

(1) We learn the connection between physical explanations and visual evolution within the latent sequence. PhysicEdit retains explicit textual reasoning and trains transition queries with a frozen reasoning MLLM. In PhysFlow, textual latents guide subsequent visual latents through causal dependencies. During planner training, downstream visual losses and the image-generation loss through the frozen generator train the earlier reasoning states (Sections 3.3 and 3.4). Physical reasoning therefore guides visual evolution and is itself shaped by the transformation it must produce.

(2) Our curriculum changes both the representation and its supervision during compression. EndoCoT supervises recurrent thought states with intermediate image-generation losses and terminal textual grounding, then shifts optimization to the terminal step; Monet distills auxiliary visual information into latent embeddings within text-latent interleaved reasoning for textual answers. PhysFlow progressively replaces textual rationales and then ordered visual blocks with latent tokens. Each visual replacement removes that block's direct alignment loss, while downstream visual and editing supervision continues to train the compressed sequence (Section 3.4). The resulting compact plan carries both forms of process reasoning into image generation without decoding textual rationales or intermediate images.

(3) PhysTrace supplies the process supervision required for joint internalization. Its 11,448 synthetic trajectories pair hierarchical physical rationales, ordered intermediate visual states, and editing targets (Section 3.2). These aligned signals extend supervision beyond source-target pairs: they explain the physical principles, trace how the scene changes, and specify the intended outcome. PhysTrace thus trains the planner on how a physical edit unfolds, as well as what it should produce.

Together, PhysFlow turns complementary textual and visual process supervision into a unified, compact latent plan trained directly for image editing.
